metadata.title: Vertex Shaders
metadata.audience: people making games in Godot, and anyone directing an AI that writes shaders for them
metadata.lecture_opening_description: How a shader moves corners to bend a shape
metadata.bookend_exempt_reason: lecture skill: opens on the narrated identity card then the hesitant writer; no composer cold open.
metadata.source_doc: Godot 4.7 documentation; Godot 4.7.2 runs on Apple M4 Pro (evidence/planning-checks); see SOURCES.md

beats.narration_text: Vertex Shaders. Learn how a shader moves the corner points of a shape, and how to give a shape enough corners to bend. By the end you can build a waving flag.

routing.reason: The lecture skill's approved first beat: portrait, title, narrated summary.

shot.visual_intent: Professor Bear portrait, exact film title and short payoff visible immediately.

show.event: Complete populated lecture opener visible for the whole narration

qc.sparse_reason: Identity card: portrait and title; teaching motion resumes in BIDEA.

beats.narration_text: Hallo. This is Liam, in for Bear. A waving flag looks as if thousands of pixels are moving. They are not. A vertex shader does not change pixels. It moves the corner points of a shape, and the graphics card fills in everything between them.
beats.motion_claim: The writer types the assumption a newcomer arrives with and corrects it into the film's real subject.

qc.sparse_reason: Hesitant-writer bookend: the correction is the motion.

beats.narration_text: Five terms. A shader is a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn. A pixel is one dot of the picture. A vertex is a corner point of a shape. A polygon is a shape made of straight edges between points. To interpolate is to blend smoothly between two known values.

terms.meaning: a small program the graphics card runs to decide how something is drawn
one dot of the picture on screen
a corner point of a shape
a shape made of straight edges between points
blend smoothly between two known values

qc.sparse_reason: TERMS card: prerequisites, one plain line each.

beats.narration_text: This flag is waving, and not one pixel in it was told to move. One line of code moves its corner points, and the graphics card fills in everything between them. That line lives in a function called vertex.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'Corners' (serif 40) top-left. A real Godot render in a framed window on the cream stage: a cream and teal checker flag pinned to a grey pole waves smoothly with its folds lit, in a seamless loop. Label: 'live clock'.

beats.narration_text: A shape is built from corner points, its vertices. The engine calls vertex once for each one, and asks a single question: where does this corner go?

shot.visual_intent: A rectangle on the cream stage with a terracotta dot on each corner. The dots flash one after another, each with a counter 1, 2, 3, 4 and a small 'where?' tag; then the four dots slide to new places and the rectangle follows as a leaning parallelogram. Caption in the GLOSSARY wording: 'vertex(): runs once for each vertex; places the corners'.

show.event: dots flash in order, counter 1 to 4

shot.motion_claim: Each corner flashes in turn with its count, then the shape follows the four moved corners.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: The count of four is the claim; four flashes in turn is the count, and the drag shows what the answer does.

beats.narration_text: The engine hands you the corner's position in a built-in, a value it gives your function. Its name is vertex too, in capital letters. Whatever you leave in it is where the corner goes.

shot.visual_intent: A box labelled vertex(). A terracotta dot labelled VERTEX (monospace) arrives from the left at the corner (-64, -64), passes through the box where the line `VERTEX.x += 40.0;` is shown, and leaves on the right at (-24, -64). Caption in the GLOSSARY wording: 'built-in: a value the engine hands to a function'.

show.event: box and the line of code

shot.motion_claim: The dot goes in, the line acts on it, and a moved dot comes out the other side.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: In and out is a flow; a dot that visibly changes on its way through says it with motion.

beats.narration_text: It counts in pixels, from the middle of the sprite. A sprite one hundred twenty-eight pixels wide has corners at minus sixty-four and sixty-four. The y axis points down, so the top corners are the minus ones.

shot.visual_intent: A 128 by 128 square with a small cross at its middle and two axis arrows drawn as shapes: x to the right, y pointing DOWN. The four corners get labels in turn: (-64, -64) top left, (64, -64) top right, (-64, 64) bottom left, (64, 64) bottom right; a scale bar '128 px'. Small grey credit: 'measured in Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+'.

show.event: y arrow pointing down is ringed

shot.motion_claim: Corner labels land one by one; the y arrow points down and the top corners carry the minus sign.

beats.narration_text: Change the number, and the corner moves. Add forty to x, and every corner moves forty pixels to the right. The whole square slides, because the graphics card fills in the shape between the moved corners.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left with the one line `VERTEX.x += 40.0;` highlighted; at right a real Godot window (640 by 360): the 128 px checker square sits still, then jumps 40 px to the right as the voice says 'add forty to x' (the shader switches on at 22 % of the beat). A terracotta ring on its new left edge, readout '+40 px'.

show.event: ring on the new left edge; +40 px

beats.narration_text: The forty is in the node's own pixels, counted before the node is scaled. Here the right-hand square is scaled to twice its size, so the same forty carries it eighty pixels across the screen.

shot.visual_intent: Same code card. At right, two real Godot squares side by side: one at its own size, one scaled to twice its size, both given the same `VERTEX.x += 40.0` at 52 % of the beat. The small one jumps 40 px, the large one 80 px. Readouts '40 px' and '80 px' under them; label 'same shader'.

beats.narration_text: Multiply, and the corners move toward or away from the middle. Here, one and a half times wider and half as tall: the square stretches and flattens. Still only four corners are moving.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left with `VERTEX *= vec2(1.5, 0.5);` highlighted; at right a real Godot window: the 128 px square, still, then at 35 % of the beat stretches to 192 px wide and flattens to 64 px tall about its middle. Readout '192×64 px'.

shot.motion_claim: The square stretches wide and flattens about its own middle when the shader switches on.

beats.narration_text: To treat corners differently, tell them apart. The engine gives each corner an address too, called U V: zero to one across, zero to one down. Top left is zero, zero. Bottom right is one, one.

shot.visual_intent: The same square, now with BOTH numberings at each corner in two rows: pixels from the middle (-64, -64) and address (0, 0), then (64, -64)/(1, 0), (-64, 64)/(0, 1), (64, 64)/(1, 1). A terracotta dot visits the corners. Caption in the GLOSSARY wording: 'UV: a point's address on the shape: 0 to 1 across, 0 to 1 down'.

show.event: top left (0, 0) and bottom right (1, 1) ringed; caption

shot.motion_claim: A dot visits the four corners and the address row of numbers lands beside each pixel row.

lecture.why: Two ways to say where one corner is is a naming claim; both labels on one square show it at a glance.

beats.narration_text: Now scale a move by the address. Add fifty times the vertical address to x. The top corners add nothing, because their address is zero. The bottom corners add fifty. The square leans.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left with `VERTEX.x += 50.0 * UV.y;` highlighted; at right a real Godot window: the 128 px checker square, still, then at 72 % of the beat it leans: the bottom edge slides 50 px right while the top stays. A terracotta ring on the bottom edge, readout '+50 px'.

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Apple M4 Pro · Forward+ · scripted: shader switched on mid-beat

shot.motion_claim: The square shears sideways when the shader switches on: top corners stay, bottom corners go fifty pixels.

lecture.why: A real shear measured to the pixel; the line and its result together are the whole lesson.
lecture.capture_spec: C05: scene `lean` of evidence/planning-checks/scratch-project/capture_scenes.gd (canvas 640 x 360): Sprite2D checker 128 px at scale 1.0; 03-lean at 0.72 of the beat; record to the event plus 1.5 s, then hold. Measured left edge 256 -> 306 (+50 px over 128 rows).

beats.narration_text: Only four corners moved. In between, the card fills the shape in even steps. We measured the left edge: fifty pixels over a hundred twenty-eight rows, on a straight line, to within half a pixel. Remember that straight line.

shot.visual_intent: The leaning square's left edge drawn as a slanted line with five sample dots along it, labelled with the measured shifts +1, +12, +25, +37 and +49 px (rows 2, 31, 63, 95 and 124 of 128). A caption: 'four corners: straight edges'. Small grey credit: 'Apple M4 Pro · Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · straight to within half a pixel'.

show.event: five dots with numbers, in order

shot.motion_claim: The five dots land one after another down the edge, each with its measured number, evenly spaced.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: The even spacing of five real measurements is the proof that nothing was calculated between the corners.

beats.narration_text: A slide, a squash, a lean: four corners are enough when the whole shape moves as one. A bend is different. Watch what a ripple does to a flag with four corners.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'More Corners' (serif 40) top-left. Three real Godot squares in a row: the left slides, the middle squashes, the right leans, all switched on together at 12 % of the beat, as the three words are said. One word under each: slide, squash, lean.

lecture.capture_spec: C06: scene `triptych` of evidence/planning-checks/scratch-project/capture_scenes.gd (canvas 640 x 360): three Sprite2D checker squares at x 130, 320, 510; shaders 01-slide, 02-squash, 03-lean at 0.12 of the beat; record to the event plus 1.5 s, then hold.

beats.narration_text: A ripple is the sine of the address across, scaled and added to y. On this flag, nothing ripples. The right end drops, and every edge stays straight.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left with `VERTEX.y += sin(UV.x * 8.0) * 24.0;` highlighted; at right a real Godot window: a cream and teal checker flag (four corners), flat for a moment, then at 58 % of the beat its right end drops 24 px and every edge stays straight: a tilt, not a ripple. Terracotta ring on the right end, readout '+24 px'. Caption: 'sine: a smooth wave between -1 and 1'.

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Apple M4 Pro · Forward+ · scripted: shader switched on mid-beat
props.caption: sine: a smooth wave between -1 and 1

shot.motion_claim: The flag does not ripple: its right end drops and the whole shape tilts, edges straight.

lecture.why: The failure is the lesson and a real render shows it honestly; a drawing could be accused of rigging it.
lecture.capture_spec: C07: scene `tilt` of evidence/planning-checks/scratch-project/capture_scenes.gd: Sprite2D flag 384 x 168 (four vertices), canvas 1280 x 720; 04-ripple assigned at 0.58 of the beat; record to the event plus 1.5 s, then hold. Measured on the Lab's 128 px sprite: right end +24 px (sin 8 x 24 = 23.7), top and bottom edges straight to within 0.49 px.

beats.narration_text: Why? Vertex can only move the vertices that exist. Between two corners, the card draws a straight line. A curve needs corners along the way, for vertex to push up and down.

shot.visual_intent: A sine curve on a grid. Two terracotta vertex dots at its ends joined by a straight chord (label '2 vertices'); then dots are added at 3, 5 and 9 positions and the chord becomes a polyline hugging the curve (labels '3', '5', '9 vertices'). A caption: 'vertex moves only the vertices that exist'.

show.event: dots added; polyline follows the curve

shot.motion_claim: More dots appear along the curve and the straight chord bends into a polyline that follows it.

lecture.why: The relation between the number of vertices and the shape they can draw is a plot, and a plot shows the chord turning into a curve.

beats.narration_text: So give the shape more vertices. Here are two ways in Godot. A polygon node, where you place the points yourself. Or a mesh node, which draws a mesh: the vertices and triangles that make a shape.

shot.visual_intent: Two panels on the cream stage. Left: a polygon outline whose points appear one at a time as if placed by hand, label 'Polygon2D: you place the points'. Right: a rectangle cut by grid lines into small cells with a dot at every crossing, label 'MeshInstance2D: a mesh cut into a grid'. Caption in the GLOSSARY wording: 'mesh: the vertices and triangles that make a shape'.
shot.motion_claim: Points appear one by one on the left while the right-hand rectangle is cut into a grid.

qc.sparse_reason: Lecture body beat: one object or scene on a cream stage, the voice carries the explanation; only underfill/clustered are waived.

lecture.why: A structure with two branches is a diagram; the reconstruction would show node names but not the vertices, which are the point.

beats.narration_text: A mesh instance two D node draws a mesh. Give it a quad mesh, a flat rectangle you can cut into a grid. Subdivide width and subdivide depth say how many extra cuts to make across and down.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left with five GDScript lines (quad mesh, size, subdivide width, subdivide depth, assign to the node); at right a real Godot window: a 320 px checker square drawn by a MeshInstance2D with terracotta dots on the mesh's vertices: four dots, then nine as the cuts go to one, then twenty-five as they go to three. Readouts '4 vertices', '9 vertices', '25 vertices'.

props.code:
var mesh := QuadMesh.new()
mesh.size = Vector2(320, 320)
mesh.subdivide_width = 3
mesh.subdivide_depth = 3
$Quad.mesh = mesh
props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · cuts raised by script · dots = the mesh's vertices
props.caption: MeshInstance2D: the node that draws a mesh in 2D

shot.motion_claim: Dots multiply on the square as the cuts are raised: four, nine, twenty-five.

lecture.why: The code and the vertices it creates side by side: the dots are the vertices, so the idea becomes countable.
lecture.capture_spec: C08: scene `mesh-recipe` of evidence/planning-checks/scratch-project/capture_scenes.gd (canvas 1280 x 720): MeshInstance2D with a QuadMesh 320 x 320, checker texture, subdivide width and depth 0 -> 1 at 0.6 of the beat -> 3 at 0.8 of the beat; a child Node2D draws a terracotta dot at every vertex of the mesh (read from surface_get_arrays); 12 s.

beats.narration_text: Count them. Cut a quad mesh three by three, and each side gets five corner points: twenty-five vertices. Always two more than the cuts, each way. The flag's thirty-one by seven makes thirty-three by nine: two hundred ninety-seven.

shot.visual_intent: A 5 by 5 grid of terracotta dots appears row by row with a running counter up to 25, labelled 'cut 3 by 3'. Beside it the formula '(cuts + 2) x (cuts + 2)'. Then the flag's 33 by 9 grid, drawn small, with its counter ending at 297, labelled 'cut 31 by 7'. Small grey credit: 'counted from the mesh in Godot 4.7.2'.
shot.motion_claim: Dots appear row by row while the counter climbs to twenty-five, then the larger grid counts to two hundred ninety-seven.

lecture.why: A count is a motion: dots appearing while a number climbs; a table would only list the results.

beats.narration_text: Same ripple. Same picture. On the left, four vertices: a tilt. On the right, two hundred ninety-seven: a ripple. Nothing in the shader changed, only how many corners it had to work with.

shot.visual_intent: Two real Godot flags side by side on the stage, the same cream and teal checker texture and the same `VERTEX.y += sin(UV.x * 8.0) * 24.0;` switched on at 10 % of the beat. Left: four vertices, the flag tilts. Right: 297 vertices, the flag ripples. Readouts '4 vertices' and '297 vertices'; label 'same shader on both'.

beats.narration_text: More vertices, a smoother wave. Four pieces show every joint. Ten soften them. Thirty-two hide them. A rule of thumb: eight pieces per wave leaves the worst gap near eight percent of the wave's height. Sixteen leaves about two.

shot.visual_intent: Three real Godot flags in a row, the same ripple switched on at 10 % of the beat, cut into 4, 10 and 32 straight pieces (subdivide width 3, 9 and 31, depth 0). The first shows every joint, the second softens them, the third has none. Readouts under them: '11 px gap', '2 px gap', 'under 1 px'. Caption: 'measured worst gap · 8 pieces per wave: about 8 % of the wave's height'.

shot.motion_claim: Three flags ripple at once; the joints are plain to see on the left and gone on the right.

beats.narration_text: Cut only where it bends. This ripple runs along the flag, never up and down, so rows of vertices add nothing. Thirty-one cuts across and none down gives sixty-six vertices, and the picture matches, pixel for pixel.

shot.visual_intent: Two real Godot flags side by side, the same ripple on at 10 % of the beat: left cut 31 by 7 (297 vertices), right cut 31 by 0 (66 vertices). They look identical. Readouts '297 vertices' and '66 vertices'; a caption 'identical, pixel for pixel'.

beats.narration_text: A polygon node gives you one vertex per point you place. With points only around the edge, Godot fills the inside with long thin triangles, and the picture twists. A grid of points, joined into cells, fixes it.

shot.visual_intent: Two real Godot flags side by side, the same ripple on at 10 % of the beat. Left: a Polygon2D with 66 points around its outline; the outline ripples but the checker inside twists along crossing lines. Right: the 297-vertex mesh, clean. A terracotta ring on the twisted crossing lines; readouts 'Polygon2D · 66 points' and 'mesh · 297 vertices'.

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Apple M4 Pro · Forward+ · scripted: shader switched on mid-beat

shot.motion_claim: Both outlines ripple, but the left flag's inside twists along long diagonal lines.

lecture.runner_up: manim: triangles drawn over the polygon
lecture.why: The twist is something you see; a drawn fan of triangles would explain it but not prove Godot does it.
lecture.capture_spec: C12: scene `polygon` of evidence/planning-checks/scratch-project/capture_scenes.gd: left Polygon2D with 66 outline points (33 on top, 33 on the bottom) and uv in texture pixels, right QuadMesh 31 x 7; 04-ripple on both at 0.1 of the beat; canvas 1280 x 720; record to the event plus 1.5 s, then hold. Verified: 64 triangles from Geometry2D.triangulate_polygon, one point in 34 of them, longest edge 419 px; the default render equals those triangles pixel for pixel; a grid of points with a cell list (polygons) equals the mesh pixel for pixel.

beats.narration_text: Now let it travel. Time is seconds on one clock shared by the whole game. Subtract it inside the sine, and the ripple slides to the right as the seconds pass.

shot.visual_intent: Act title 'A Waving Flag' (serif 40) top-left. Code card at left with `VERTEX.y += sin(UV.x * 8.0 - TIME * 3.0) * 24.0;` highlighted; at right a real Godot window: the mesh flag on a grey pole shows the static ripple, then at the 58 % mark the ripple starts to slide to the right. Caption in the GLOSSARY wording: 'TIME: seconds on one clock shared by the whole game'.

props.videoLabel: Godot 4.7.2 · Forward+ · live clock · scripted: shader switched on at 58 % of the beat
props.caption: TIME: seconds on one clock shared by the whole game
props.title: A Waving Flag

shot.motion_claim: A frozen ripple starts to travel to the right along the flag, the left end bobbing with it.

lecture.runner_up: manim sine plot with a phase marker
lecture.why: A ripple that starts to move on the real flag is the claim; the plot would only describe the phase.
lecture.capture_spec: C13: scene `travel` of evidence/planning-checks/scratch-project/capture_scenes.gd: MeshInstance2D flag (QuadMesh 384 x 168 cut 31 x 7) with a grey pole at the left edge; 04-ripple from the start, 05-flag-travelling assigned at 0.58 of the beat; canvas 1280 x 720; record the whole beat (D) and hold. Verified: the wave moves right as TIME grows (fitted phase advanced with the clock; mean error 0.25 px).

beats.narration_text: But a flag is held at one end. Multiply the ripple by the address across. At the left edge the address is zero, so nothing is added, and that edge stays put, like a pole.

shot.visual_intent: Code card at left with `VERTEX.y += sin(UV.x * 8.0 - TIME * 3.0) * 24.0 * UV.x;` and the final `* UV.x` highlighted; at right a real Godot window: the travelling flag bobs at its left end as well; at the 30 % mark the new line goes on and the left end, beside the grey pole, stops moving while the rest keeps rippling. A terracotta ring on the left edge, readout 'pinned'.

shot.motion_claim: The left edge stops moving the moment the multiplication goes on; the rest of the flag keeps waving.

lecture.why: A real flag losing its flapping at the pole end is the picture of 'held at one end'.

beats.narration_text: Three numbers shape the wave: how tall, how many waves fit, how fast. Make each a uniform: a value your game sets from outside the shader, the same for every vertex and pixel. Now the flag has three dials.

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. Vertex runs once for each corner and decides where it goes. A shape can only bend where it has vertices. Cut a mesh until each wave has eight pieces or more. A flag is a sine of the address and the time, pinned at one end, with dials. A varying carries a value from the corners to every pixel. When it looks wrong, count the vertices, and check what each position is measured from.

A shape can only bend where it has vertices.
Cut a mesh until each wave has eight pieces or more.
A flag is a sine of the address and the time, pinned at one end, with dials.
A varying carries a value from the corners to every pixel.
When it looks wrong, count the vertices, and check what each position is measured from.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude: Write a Godot canvas item shader for a waving banner. Draw it with a MeshInstance two D and a quad mesh cut thirty-one by seven. In vertex, move the corners up and down with a sine of the address across and the time. Make amplitude, frequency and speed float uniforms, and pin the left edge. Then tell me how many vertices the mesh has. Then check two things yourself. Does the left edge stay still while the rest ripples? And does the vertex count match thirty-three by nine?
